食べてる.note: The い just drops. This one even survives into polite speech: 食べてます is normal in almost any conversation.

何してんの.note: 〜ているの → 〜てんの (and を drops on the way). The る before の collapses to ん everywhere: やってるの→やってんの, 言ってるの→言ってんの.

読んどく.note: 〜ておく→〜とく, 〜でおく→〜どく. 買っておく→買っとく, やっておく→やっとく.

忘れちゃった.note: 〜てしまう→〜ちゃう. It carries either 'completely' or 'oops' — here, clearly oops.

飲んじゃう.note: After the voiced て-forms it is 〜でしまう→〜じゃう: 読んじゃう, 死んじゃう.

行かなきゃ.note: Usually the sentence stops right there, with いけない left unsaid. Finishing it (行かなきゃいけない) sounds more deliberate.

行かなくちゃ.note: 〜なくては→〜なくちゃ. Interchangeable with なきゃ; なくちゃ feels slightly softer and a touch more feminine, but only slightly.

わかんない.note: ら→ん before ない. Same with つまらない→つまんない, 変わらない→変わんない, 信じられない→信じらんない.

学生じゃない.note: ではない→じゃない is so complete that ではない now reads as written or oratorical, not merely polite.

食べれる.note: ら抜き言葉. Standard in speech across every age group now, and still marked wrong in writing and by some older people. Note it makes 'can eat' and 'is eaten' distinguishable, which is why it won.

すげえ.note: 〜ai crushes to 〜ee: うまい→うめえ, やばい→やべえ, 高い→たけえ. Rough and strongly male. Women use it, but usually for comic effect.

てか.note: Opens a sentence that redirects what was just said. てゆーか and つーか are the same word; てか is the shortest and most common in texts.

それじゃ.note: The same squeeze keeps going: それでは→それじゃ→じゃあ→じゃ. All four are alive, in descending order of formality.

ほんとに.note: Spelled ほんとう, said ほんと by nearly everyone. ほんっとに with the small っ is the emphatic version.

すいません.note: すいません is how most people actually pronounce it. Perfectly normal spoken, but write すみません.

や.note: One syllable carries most of the dialect. だから→やから, だけど→やけど, だろう→やろ, なんだ→なんや.

せや.note: せや is the Osaka default; そや and ほや also occur. ほな (= それじゃあ) uses the same ほ: ほな、また明日.

そや.note: せや is the Osaka default; そや and ほや also occur. ほな (= それじゃあ) uses the same ほ: ほな、また明日.

ええ.note: Only the dictionary form changes. The past is still よかった, and the negative is ようない (よくない is heard too). ええ天気やな.

てる.note: 〜てる is neutral. 〜とる is rougher and more male in Osaka — 何しとん？ can land as a challenge where 何してん？ does not.

とる.note: 〜てる is neutral. 〜とる is rougher and more male in Osaka — 何しとん？ can land as a challenge where 何してん？ does not.

てまう.note: Past 〜てもた: 忘れてもた. Tokyo's 〜ちゃった is understood perfectly well in Kansai but sounds imported. Separately, note that standalone ちゃう in Kansai is 違う — a different word that only looks related.

なあかん.note: 行かなあかん. There is no everyday polite version — for 〜なければなりません even lifelong Osakans switch to 標準語.

んとあかん.note: 行かなあかん. There is no everyday polite version — for 〜なければなりません even lifelong Osakans switch to 標準語.

たらあかん.note: 触ったらあかんで. あかん covers everything だめ covers.

んでもええ.note: 行かんでもええ. The plain Kansai negative stem is 〜ん: 知らん, わからん, 行かん.

やろ.note: やろ？ fishes for agreement, やろな muses. It is plain speech — not a stand-in for でしょう with someone senior.

どない.note: どないする？, どないしたん？, どないやねん. どう is still said; どない is the marked local one.

はよ.note: Kansai keeps the old ウ音便 — adverbial 〜く becomes 〜う and fuses. 早く→はよう→はよ, よく→よう. はよ行こ.

たこうなる.note: The same change before なる: 安くなる→やすうなる. Strongest in older speakers; younger Osakans often just say 高くなる.

言うた.note: う-verbs take ウ音便 in the past and the て-form: 言うた (ゆうた), 買うてくる, 思うてた. The change learners never notice they are missing.

こうた.note: う-verbs take ウ音便 in the past and the て-form: 言うた (ゆうた), 買うてくる, 思うてた. The change learners never notice they are missing.

し.note: For 一段 verbs and する the Kansai imperative is the ます-stem, usually softened with や: はよしいや, ちょっと見いや. 五段 verbs keep the standard imperative — 行け, 飲め — and take や on the stem instead: 行きや. Downward only, parent to child or friend to friend.

見い.note: For 一段 verbs and する the Kansai imperative is the ます-stem, usually softened with や: はよしいや, ちょっと見いや. 五段 verbs keep the standard imperative — 行け, 飲め — and take や on the stem instead: 行きや. Downward only, parent to child or friend to friend.

行かへん.note: For 五段 verbs 〜へん sits on the same stem as 〜ない. Osaka also says 行けへん for this — it looks like the potential and is not.

わからへん.note: わからん and 知らん are the everyday forms; the へん versions come out a little softer.

食べへん.note: 一段 verbs drop る and add へん: 寝へん, 起きへん.

見いひん.note: After an い vowel へん often becomes ひん and the stem stretches: 見いひん, 起きひん, できひん. This is a tendency, not a rule — 見えへん is just as current in Osaka — and Kyoto uses ひん more widely than Osaka does.

せえへん.note: せえへん is Osaka, しいひん Kyoto, せん the wider western form. All three are current.

しいひん.note: せえへん is Osaka, しいひん Kyoto, せん the wider western form. All three are current.

こーへん.note: こーへん is Osaka, きーひん Kyoto, けーへん Kobe. This one word tells a local exactly where you learned your Japanese.

きーひん.note: こーへん is Osaka, きーひん Kyoto, けーへん Kobe. This one word tells a local exactly where you learned your Japanese.

お金あらへん.note: ある has no 〜ん negative of its own — plain ない does that job. あらへん and あれへん are the same emphatic word, where ない is flat.

でけへん.note: The stem shifts to でけ〜, not でき〜 — though younger speakers do say できひん.

食べてへん.note: 〜とらん is the negative of 〜とる: rougher in Osaka, but the normal form further west.

行かんといて.note: Both are built on 〜ん, not on へん, and both are warm rather than sharp: 言わんといてや. If anything 〜んとって is the more coaxing of the two, not the blunter.

行かへんかった.note: Kansai adds かった to the whole negative instead of inflecting ない.

そうちゃう.note: Neither of these is a へん form: そうちゃう uses ちゃう (= 違う) and そうやない is や + ない. Both are current, and ちゃう also stands alone as a flat 'no, wrong'.

行かん.note: For 五段 verbs 〜へん sits on the same stem as 〜ない. Osaka also says 行けへん for this — it looks like the potential and is not.

わからん.note: わからん and 知らん are the everyday forms; the へん versions come out a little softer.

食べん.note: 一段 verbs drop る and add へん: 寝へん, 起きへん.

見ん.note: After an い vowel へん often becomes ひん and the stem stretches: 見いひん, 起きひん, できひん. This is a tendency, not a rule — 見えへん is just as current in Osaka — and Kyoto uses ひん more widely than Osaka does.

せん.note: せえへん is Osaka, しいひん Kyoto, せん the wider western form. All three are current.

こん.note: こーへん is Osaka, きーひん Kyoto, けーへん Kobe. This one word tells a local exactly where you learned your Japanese.

お金ない.note: ある has no 〜ん negative of its own — plain ない does that job. あらへん and あれへん are the same emphatic word, where ない is flat.

でけん.note: The stem shifts to でけ〜, not でき〜 — though younger speakers do say できひん.

食べとらん.note: 〜とらん is the negative of 〜とる: rougher in Osaka, but the normal form further west.

行かんとって.note: Both are built on 〜ん, not on へん, and both are warm rather than sharp: 言わんといてや. If anything 〜んとって is the more coaxing of the two, not the blunter.

行かんかった.note: Kansai adds かった to the whole negative instead of inflecting ない.

そうやない.note: Neither of these is a へん form: そうちゃう uses ちゃう (= 違う) and そうやない is や + ない. Both are current, and ちゃう also stands alone as a flat 'no, wrong'.

明日行くねん.note: ねん is 〜んだ/〜のだ — it explains rather than just states. The most Kansai-marking ending there is, and the one learners overuse first.

すごいやん.note: やん = じゃない(か) and clips onto plain forms: ええやん, 行くやん. やんか pushes back: 言うたやんか, 'I did tell you.'

おいしいで.note: で is Kansai's よ — informing, not swaggering. Unlike Tokyo's ぜ it is used by women and older speakers just as much.

せやな.note: な does the work of ね throughout: ええ天気やな, 疲れたな.

知らんわ.note: Kansai わ is flat and gender-neutral, and men use it constantly. It is not the rising, feminine わ of Tokyo speech.

帰ろか.note: 〜か on the volitional is a soft invitation: ぼちぼち行こか.

あかんて.note: 〜て is 〜って — reporting or insisting. 言うてるやん, 'I keep telling you.'

待ってえな.note: 〜えな and 〜や turn a request into a wheedle: 教えてえな, 見してや. Friends only; it sounds childish upwards.

ちゃうがな.note: がな is heavy old-Osaka — mostly older men and comedians now. Understand it; you do not need it.

行ぐべ.note: 〜べ marks intention or a guess; the copula version is 〜だべ. The く→ぐ voicing between vowels is Tohoku specifically — North Kanto says 行くべ.

東京さ行ぐ.note: さ replaces へ and に. Tohoku speech is sometimes subtitled on national television, which locals find as patronising as it sounds.

こわい.note: Not 'scary'. A real false friend that causes real confusion.

なまら美味い.note: なまら is the Hokkaido intensifier. 〜っしょ (from でしょ) is the other giveaway.

投げる.note: ゴミ投げといて means bin it, not hurl it.

そうばい.note: 〜たい states the speaker's own view; 〜ばい presents it to the listener as news. Both are everyday Hakata.

好いとう.en: I like it / I like you
好いとう.note: 好いとう (好いとぉ) is the statement. Add と for the question: 好いとーと？ — 〜と？ is the general Kyushu question ending, as in 行くと？

ばり速か.note: ばり is Hakata's intensifier, and 〜か is the local adjective ending (速か, よか). Osaka would say めっちゃ, Hiroshima ぶち.

じゃ.note: じゃけえ ('because') is the signature. Gangster films made 広島弁 the voice of screen yakuza; it is an ordinary regional dialect with an unfair reputation.

ぶち寒い.note: ぶち is the local とても: ぶちうまい, ぶち寒い.

そうだがや.note: だがや and みゃー are the television version. Actual Nagoya speech today is close to 標準語, with 〜だがね and 〜がや surviving in casual talk.

えらい.note: Three regions, three meanings: Nagoya えらい = tired, Kansai えらい = awfully (えらい人多いな), standard えらい = admirable. Context decides which one you are hearing.

めんそーれ.note: Okinawan is not a dialect the way Kansai is — it separated early enough that the two are not mutually intelligible. It gets a module of its own in this stage.
